issues.legal_issue: The appeal does not abate as a whole when deceased plaintiffs’ unrepresented interests concern management of property.
material_facts: Some plaintiffs died while the appeal was pending, and their legal representatives were not brought on record.
The plaintiffs had been held to be descendants of the property’s Mutawalis, whose position was managerial.
issues.conclusion: The appeal did not abate as a whole because the interests in question were managerial in nature.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the Mutawali position as a managerial post and held that the deaths and failure to substitute the deceased plaintiffs’ legal representatives did not cause the appeal as a whole to abate.

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the disputed property is pending.
predicates.deceased_claimants_not_substituted: Some claimants have died during the appeal and their legal representatives have not been brought on record.
predicates.claim_concerns_managerial_position: The claimants’ relevant interest concerns a managerial position relating to the property.

issues.definition: When an appeal is pending, deceased claimants have not been substituted, and their claim concerns a managerial position, the appeal does not abate as a whole.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings on title supported by evidence are not disturbed where no question of law arises.
material_facts: The trial court’s dismissal was reversed by the first appellate court, which found that the land belonged to the religious institution and that the plaintiffs and another defendant were entitled to the relevant status.
The High Court confirmed the finding that the land belonged to the religious institution, relying on documentary records showing the land associated with it over many years.
The Supreme Court found that the concurrent findings were based on evidence and that no question of law arose concerning ownership.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding concerning ownership was a finding of fact and was not disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to interfere with concurrent factual findings on ownership that were based on evidence and raised no question of law.

rule.if: supreme_court_civil_appeal and concurrent_title_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and no_question_of_law_on_title

predicates.supreme_court_civil_appeal: The matter is a civil appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.concurrent_title_findings: The lower appellate courts have made the same finding about title to the property.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The title findings rest on evidence in the record.
predicates.no_question_of_law_on_title: The title dispute presents no question of law.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, concurrent title findings supported by evidence are not disturbed when the title dispute presents no question of law.

issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking possession based on title is governed by the limitation applicable to title-based possession even when it also seeks a declaration.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought both a declaration concerning their rights and possession of the land based on title.
Possession was handed over to the opposing side in 1978, and the suit was filed in 1987.
The appellants argued that the three-year limitation for a declaratory suit applied.
issues.conclusion: The suit was governed by Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and was within limitation because it was filed within twelve years of the possession becoming adverse.
issues.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a twelve-year limitation period for a suit for possession of immovable property based on title, running from when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse. A declaration sought as part of such a possession suit does not make the suit one governed by the shorter period for a declaration alone. The Court distinguished L.C. Hanumanthappa v. H.B. Shivakumar, (2016) 1 SCC 332, because that was a suit for declaration alone, not for both declaration and possession.

predicates.possession_suit_based_on_title: The claimant seeks possession of immovable property on the basis of title.
predicates.declaration_also_claimed: The claimant also seeks a declaration concerning title or rights in the property.
predicates.filed_within_adverse_possession_period: The suit is filed within the applicable period measured from when the opposing possession became adverse.

issues.definition: A title-based possession suit that also seeks a declaration is within limitation when filed within the applicable period measured from the start of adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: A court may grant a lesser status encompassed by the higher status claimed, even if the lesser status was not separately pleaded as the relief sought.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed the higher status of Inamdars.
The High Court found that they were descendants of Mutawalis rather than Inamdars.
The Court considered Mutawali status to be a lesser relief than the status claimed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could grant the lesser relief of recognising the plaintiffs as Mutawalis, and had not granted a wholly new or higher relief.
issues.legal_principle: A court may grant a lesser or smaller version of the relief claimed, but may not ignore the prayer and grant an unrelated relief. The Court applied Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal, (2008) 17 SCC 491, and held that recognition as Mutawalis was a lesser relief than the claimed status of Inamdars.

rule.if: civil_suit and higher_status_claimed and evidence_supports_lesser_status and lesser_status_is_within_claimed_relief

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking relief concerning the claimant’s status or rights.
predicates.higher_status_claimed: The claimant seeks recognition of a higher status.
predicates.evidence_supports_lesser_status: The evidence supports recognition of a lower status instead of the higher status claimed.
predicates.lesser_status_is_within_claimed_relief: The lower status is a lesser version of, rather than a wholly different relief from, the status claimed.

issues.definition: In a civil suit, when the evidence supports a lower status that is a lesser version of the higher status claimed, the court may grant that lesser status.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court has jurisdiction over a dispute about whether property belongs to a religious institution when the claim concerns management rights rather than whether the property is wakf property.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether the land belonged to the religious institution.
The plaintiffs claimed rights to manage the institution’s property and did not claim a personal right in the land.
The issue was not whether the land was wakf property.
No objection to civil-court jurisdiction had been raised before the trial court, though it was raised before the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to decide the suit.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a dispute about whether property belongs to a religious institution from a determination of whether property is wakf property. Because the claim concerned management rights over the institution’s property and not personal rights in the land, the civil court had jurisdiction.

rule.if: civil_suit and dispute_concerns_institution_property_ownership and claim_concerns_management_rights and dispute_not_about_wakf_status

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.dispute_concerns_institution_property_ow: The dispute is whether property belongs to a religious institution.
predicates.claim_concerns_management_rights: The claimant asserts rights to manage the institution’s property rather than personal rights in the land.
predicates.dispute_not_about_wakf_status: The dispute is not about determining whether the property is wakf property.

issues.definition: A civil court has jurisdiction over a civil suit about ownership of an institution’s property when the claim concerns management rights and the dispute is not about wakf status.

issues.legal_issue: Documents first tendered during a Supreme Court appeal may be rejected when the applicant gives no reason for failing to produce them earlier and does not satisfy the requirements for additional evidence.
material_facts: The appellants applied during the appeal to place documents on record that had not been produced before the trial court.
They gave no explanation for not producing the documents earlier.

They had not applied to lead additional evidence before the first appellate court or the High Court, and their applications did not meet the requirements of Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
issues.conclusion: The applications were rejected, and the documents were not taken into consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, additional evidence must satisfy the rule’s requirements. The Court rejected documents sought to be introduced at the appeal stage when they had not been produced earlier, no explanation was given for that omission, and the applications did not meet those requirements.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and additional_documents_first_tendered_on_appeal and documents_not_produced_earlier and no_explanation_for_earlier_omission and additional_evidence_requirements_not_met

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.additional_documents_first_tendered_on_a: A party applies during the appeal to add documents to the record.
predicates.documents_not_produced_earlier: The documents were not produced before the trial court or in the earlier appellate proceedings.
predicates.no_explanation_for_earlier_omission: The applicant gives no reason for failing to produce the documents earlier.
predicates.additional_evidence_requirements_not_met: The application does not satisfy the requirements for receiving additional evidence.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, documents first tendered on appeal are rejected when they were not produced earlier, the omission is unexplained, and the requirements for additional evidence are unmet.
